stichs.en: Forever, LORD,
Your word stands firm in the heavens.

verses.summary: Lamed opens with davar, the word, and with no request at all. The claim is that the word is already fixed in heaven, older than the speaker's need of it.

stichs.en: To generation after generation is Your faithfulness;
You established the earth, and it stands.

verses.summary: One of the two verses in the psalm that use none of the eight Torah words. Faithfulness stands in their place, and the proof offered is the earth, which was set up and simply keeps standing.

stichs.en: By Your judgments they stand today,
for everything is Your servant.

verses.summary: Mishpatim, the judgments, read cosmically. The same rulings that govern the speaker hold the day in place, and every created thing is enrolled as a servant.

stichs.en: Had Your teaching not been my delight,
I would then have perished in my affliction.

verses.summary: The first counterfactual of the stanza. Torah is called sha'ashua, delight, and the claim is bare survival: without that delight the affliction would already have finished him.

stichs.en: Never will I forget Your precepts,
for through them You have kept me alive.

verses.summary: Pikudim, precepts, joined to a promise never to forget. The reason arrives in a single word, through them, which credits the precepts themselves with keeping him alive.

stichs.en: I am Yours, save me,
for I have sought Your precepts.

verses.summary: The shortest possession claim in the psalm: I am Yours. The imperative hoshieni, save me, rests on that ownership and on the fact that he went looking for the pikudim.

stichs.en: The wicked have lain in wait for me to destroy me;
I study Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Two parties wait at once. They wait to destroy, and while they wait he studies the edot, so the ambush is answered by attention rather than by flight.

stichs.en: To all perfection I have seen an end;
Your commandment is exceedingly broad.

verses.summary: The one verse here that measures Torah against everything else. He has found a limit to all completeness; only the mitzvah is called broad, and exceedingly is the last word of the stanza.

stichs.en: How I love Your teaching!
All the day it is my meditation.

verses.summary: Mem opens with an exclamation, not a petition. Torah is loved and named sichah, the thing he talks over all day, which sets up the three comparisons that follow.

stichs.en: Wiser than my enemies Your commandments make me,
for they are mine forever.

verses.summary: First of three comparisons: wiser than enemies. The mitzvot are the instrument, and the singular pronoun treats them as one possession that never leaves him.

stichs.en: More than all my teachers I have grown wise,
for Your testimonies are my meditation.

verses.summary: Second comparison, and the risky one: more insight than his teachers. The edot are what he keeps talking over, so the claim is about attention, not native talent.

stichs.en: More than elders I understand,
because I have kept Your precepts.

verses.summary: Third comparison, the elders, and here the reason shifts from meditation to conduct: he understands because he has guarded the pikudim, not because he has thought harder.

stichs.en: From every evil path I have held back my feet,
so that I may keep Your word.

verses.summary: A negative discipline. Feet held back from every evil path, with lema'an, in order that, making the restraint purposeful: it exists so the davar can be kept.

stichs.en: From Your judgments I have not turned aside,
for You Yourself have taught me.

verses.summary: The paired negative: no turning aside from the mishpatim. The reason is handed to God as teacher, so standing still is not counted as the speaker's own achievement.

stichs.en: How smooth to my palate is Your saying,
sweeter than honey to my mouth.

verses.summary: The taste verse. Imrah, the saying, is placed on the palate and rated against honey, the only place in this stretch where Torah is measured by a sense rather than an argument.

stichs.en: From Your precepts I gain understanding;
therefore I hate every false path.

verses.summary: Mem closes the way it argued. Understanding comes out of the pikudim, and that understanding produces hatred of every false path, so knowledge here has a moral edge and not only a scope.

stichs.en: A lamp for my foot is Your word,
and a light for my path.

verses.summary: Nun opens with the most quoted line of the psalm. Davar as a lamp is small, local light, enough for one step, which is exactly what a foot needs.

stichs.en: I have sworn, and I will fulfill it,
to keep the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: A verse of oath. The unusual doubling, sworn and then confirmed, binds him twice over to the mishpatim, which are named here as the judgments of Your righteousness.

stichs.en: I am afflicted very much;
LORD, give me life according to Your word.

verses.summary: The first plain complaint of the stanza. Affliction is stated with no cause given, and the request chayeni, give me life, is measured strictly by the davar.

stichs.en: Accept, please, the freewill offerings of my mouth, LORD,
and teach me Your judgments.

verses.summary: Sacrificial language borrowed for speech: what he brings are the freewill offerings of his mouth. The second half asks for instruction in the mishpatim, so praise and learning arrive in one breath.

stichs.en: My soul is in my palm continually,
yet Your teaching I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: Life carried in the palm is an idiom for constant danger. The counterweight is memory: even so, the torah has not been forgotten, and that contrast is the whole line.

stichs.en: The wicked have set a trap for me,
yet from Your precepts I have not strayed.

verses.summary: The danger of verse 109 becomes concrete, a trap laid by the wicked. The answering verb is not escape but not straying from the pikudim, so staying on course is the survival move.

stichs.en: I have taken Your testimonies as my inheritance forever,
for they are the joy of my heart.

verses.summary: The vocabulary turns legal. The edot are taken as a nachalah, an inherited holding rather than a duty, and the reason given for wanting it is joy.

stichs.en: I have inclined my heart to do Your statutes,
forever, to the very end.

verses.summary: Nun closes on an act of will: the heart bent toward doing the chukim. The last word fixes the term, all the way to the end, giving the stanza a horizon rather than a mood.

stichs.en: The divided I hate,
but Your teaching I love.

verses.summary: Samech opens on a hated object, the divided or half hearted, set directly opposite love of the torah. Four words, two verbs, and the stanza's theme of separation is already set.

stichs.en: My hiding place and my shield are You;
for Your word I wait.

verses.summary: Two shelter nouns, then a verb of waiting. Nothing is actually requested: the davar is what he waits on, and the waiting is offered as the response to danger.

stichs.en: Turn away from me, you evildoers,
that I may keep the commandments of my God.

verses.summary: The rare imperative addressed to people rather than to God. Evildoers are told to leave, and the stated purpose is keeping the mitzvot, so company is treated as an obstacle to practice.

stichs.en: Uphold me according to Your saying, that I may live,
and do not let me be shamed of my hope.

verses.summary: Two requests fused into one: hold me up by the imrah so that I live, and do not let my hope be disgraced. Living and not being shamed are asked for as the same favour.

stichs.en: Support me, that I may be saved,
and I will gaze on Your statutes continually.

verses.summary: Rescue asked for with a purpose clause attached. Held upright, he can keep looking at the chukim without stopping, so being saved is wanted in order that study can continue.

stichs.en: You have set aside all who stray from Your statutes,
for their deceit is falsehood.

verses.summary: The judgment half of the stanza. Those who wander from the chukim are set aside, and the reason given is that their cleverness is a lie, not that they are weak.

stichs.en: Like dross You have removed all the wicked of the earth;
therefore I love Your testimonies.

verses.summary: A metallurgical image: the wicked skimmed off like the scum on molten metal. The speaker draws his own conclusion from it, love of the edot, so the verse ends with him and not with them.

stichs.en: My flesh bristles in dread of You,
and of Your judgments I am afraid.

verses.summary: Samech ends in the body. Flesh bristles, and the object of the dread is the mishpatim themselves, which turns the judgment of verse 118 back onto the speaker.

stichs.en: I have done justice and righteousness;
do not leave me to my oppressors.

verses.summary: Ayin opens with a claim of merit, rare in this psalm. Having done mishpat himself, all he asks is not to be handed over to those pressing him.

stichs.en: Stand surety for Your servant for good;
let the arrogant not oppress me.

verses.summary: The second of the two verses using none of the eight Torah words. It asks God to act as guarantor for His own servant, a term taken from debt law rather than from Torah.

stichs.en: My eyes have failed for Your salvation,
and for the saying of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: Eyes giving out is the idiom for waiting past endurance. Two things are awaited at once, the salvation and the imrah, which makes rescue and word a single expected arrival.

stichs.en: Deal with Your servant according to Your kindness,
and teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The measure named for the request is chesed, kindness, not the record claimed back in verse 121. What that kindness is asked to buy is instruction in the chukim.

stichs.en: I am Your servant, give me understanding,
that I may know Your testimonies.

verses.summary: The servant title of verse 122 turned into leverage for a request. Understanding is asked for with an explicit purpose attached: so that the edot can be known.

stichs.en: It is time to act for the LORD;
they have broken Your teaching.

verses.summary: The one verse in this stretch that speaks of God in the third person, and it tells Him when to move. The ground offered is that people have annulled the torah.

stichs.en: Therefore I love Your commandments
more than gold, more than fine gold.

verses.summary: The gold comparison. Mitzvot outrank both zahav and paz, the ordinary metal and the refined one, which is the only economic measure the ayin stanza uses.

stichs.en: Therefore all the precepts of everything I hold to be right;
every false path I hate.

verses.summary: The most emphatic verse of the stanza, with kol, all, appearing three times in ten words. Every one of the pikudim is declared straight, and the matching move is hatred of every false path.

stichs.en: Wonders are Your testimonies;
therefore my soul has kept them.

verses.summary: Pe opens by calling the edot wonders, the vocabulary of miracle rather than of law. What follows is guarding, and the guardian named is the nefesh itself.

stichs.en: The opening of Your words gives light,
giving understanding to the simple.

verses.summary: The teaching verse. What gives light is the petach, the opening or unfolding of the words, and the beneficiaries named are the simple rather than the learned.

stichs.en: I opened my mouth wide and panted,
for I longed for Your commandments.

verses.summary: A physical image of appetite, the mouth wide and the breath short. The object of the craving is the mitzvot, so desire and not duty is given as the reason for keeping them.

stichs.en: Turn to me and be gracious to me,
as is the rule for those who love Your name.

verses.summary: The turn to face. Two imperatives, turn and show favour, and the standard invoked is mishpat in its sense of customary practice, what is owed to those who love the Name.
